subjects.introduction: Bahá’u’lláh calls martyrdom a rare elixir that no one may seek for himself, and in the same breath commands wisdom, forbids the taking of one’s own life and praises those who let themselves be killed rather than kill. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá explains that the longing itself is the martyrdom, so that a teacher or a parent who surrenders self-will already walks the road the martyrs of Yazd and Nayriz walked; the kin of the slain, he adds, are martyred every day and owed the community’s care. Honoring the dead becomes responsibility for the living, and remembrance turns into schooling, relief and trustworthy conduct. The road leads back to Imam Husayn and the martyrdom of the Báb, outward into consolation and comfort for the grieving, and inward through the mystery of sacrifice and the tests and trials that form character. Paul’s counsel to bless persecutors and feed an enemy [1], the Qur’an’s assurance that those slain in God’s cause live with their Lord [2] and the Dhammapada’s turn from every creature’s love of life to the refusal of violence [3] keep these questions honest.

shortened: O army of God! The Exalted One, the Bab, gave up His life. The Blessed Perfection gave up a hundred lives at every breath. He bore calamities. He suffered anguish. He was imprisoned. He was chained. He was made homeless and was banished to distant lands. Finally, then, He lived out His days in the Most Great Prison. Likewise, a great multitude of the lovers of God who followed this path have tasted the honey of martyrdom and they gave up everything -- life, possessions, kindred -- all they had.

Forgiveness and personal nonretaliation also appear alongside appeals for protection and distinctions concerning public justice; keep each statement in its setting. How might steadfastness include avoiding danger, seeking help or postponing a journey? What would prevent admiration for sacrifice from becoming an expectation that someone else should suffer? The accounts of early conflict, the different devotional languages of the sources and later prohibitions of warfare should each remain visible.

order.why: Consider what the texts mean by witness, sacrifice and the recognition of God. Images of a chalice, a flame, a seed or an offering connect suffering with love and enduring life, yet they do not all describe the same event. Read the accounts of Husayn, the Bab and Baha’u’llah with their own voices and theological claims intact. Some passages praise a death endured faithfully; others describe the relinquishment of self-will before any outward death. How does an image disclose meaning, and where might a literal reading conceal it? Attend also to the distinction between spiritual detachment and abandonment of useful work or family responsibility.
shortened: As to what thou hast mentioned concerning martyrdom, know thou that it hath manifold degrees. We shall impart unto thee that which ye are able to understand. Among them is the station of thy bearing witness unto thy Lord, wherein thou beholdest Him standing over all things, and art among those who with feet of steel stand firm in the valley of steadfastness.

Among them is the degree of martyrdom at the time when the Herald of the Spirit calleth out from behind the veils of holiness: "Arise to aid God, O ye sincere ones!" that ye may strive in the path of God until ye sacrifice yourselves in His love, finding in this the utmost delight from the core of your hearts.

order.why: End the linked readings with their accounts of eternal life, divine grace and continuing relation.
